headline: Fed raises rates for the first time in three years
summary: The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate a quarter point Wednesday, to 3.75%-4%, its first increase since July 2023. The vote was unanimous. Chair Kevin Warsh said inflation "is too high and has been for too long." Trump, who picked Warsh, posted that rates should be 1% or less. Most Fed officials expect another hike this year.

cover_question.q: Can the president overrule the Fed?

cover_answer: No. The Fed is independent, and it raised them anyway.
table_question: Would you tell the person who gave you your job that they're wrong?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The bank that sets money rules for the whole country made borrowing cost a little more. Borrowing is like getting a toy from a friend and giving back a little extra as thanks. That extra just got a tiny bit bigger, to help stop store prices from climbing so fast. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Interest is abstract. A borrowed toy with a thank-you attached is not.
5-7.why_long: Interest is an abstraction and a five-year-old will not get there. A borrowed toy handed back with something extra is one they can hold, and the script never leaves it. Why it matters gets one clause and no more. Expect “do we have to pay more?” On a loan, yes. On a toy, no.

8-12.script: Prices have risen faster than the Fed wants for five years. On Wednesday the Fed raised interest rates, so loans and credit cards cost more. People borrow less, buy less, and prices climb more slowly. Like a thermostat: too hot, so they turned the heat down.
8-12.why: Rates to spending to prices is one chain they can follow.
8-12.why_long: Rates to borrowing to spending to prices. Four links, which is a lot, so the script gives the thermostat to hold them together: too hot, turn it down. Ten-year-olds like a control they can see. Expect “why not just tell shops to charge less?” Because nobody can, and that is worth saying out loud.

13-17.script: Can the president overrule the Fed? Trump picked Kevin Warsh to run it and wants rates at 1% or less. Warsh raised them anyway, in a unanimous vote, saying inflation "is too high and has been for too long." Should the Fed answer to voters, or stay out of politics?
13-17.why: Teens get the boss-versus-expert tension. Let them pick a side first.
13-17.why_long: Trump picked Warsh and Warsh did the opposite, unanimously. A teenager can hold the appointment and the defiance together and see the design in it. The script asks whether the Fed should answer to voters at all. Ask which they would choose before you say. There is a real case on both sides.

5-7.a: A little more if we borrow, like on a credit card. A little more for us if we save. Nothing changes at dinner tonight.

8-12.a: The extra you pay to borrow money, as a share of the loan. Higher rates make loans and credit cards cost more.

8-12.q: Why is Trump mad about it?
8-12.a: He wants rates cut to 1% or less. He picked the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, but the Fed decides on its own, and the vote was unanimous.

13-17.q: Can the president overrule the Fed?
13-17.a: No. The Fed is independent of the government. Trump can criticize it, and did, but the rate vote was unanimous and it stands.

13-17.q: Should the Fed answer to voters?
13-17.a: Warsh's line is that independence means the Fed stays in its lane. The White House says the president can still voice his opinion.
